claims: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes (meninges) surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Meningitis is usually caused by viral or bacterial infections.
High fever is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
Stiff neck is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
Severe headache is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
Nausea/vomiting is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
Sensitivity to light is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
Confusion is a symptom of meningitis in adults.
A rash is sometimes a symptom of meningitis in adults.
High fever is a symptom of meningitis in infants.
Constant crying is a symptom of meningitis in infants.
Extreme sleepiness or irritability is a symptom of meningitis in infants.
Poor feeding is a symptom of meningitis in infants.
A bulge in the soft spot (fontanelle) is a symptom of meningitis in infants.
Viral meningitis is the most common type.
Viral meningitis is often less severe.
Bacterial meningitis is rare.
Bacterial meningitis is severe.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common bacterium for bacterial meningitis.
Neisseria meningitidis is a common bacterium for bacterial meningitis.
Fungal infections can cause meningitis.
Parasitic infections can cause meningitis.
Amoebic infections can cause meningitis.
Cancers are non-infectious causes of meningitis.
Injuries are non-infectious causes of meningitis.
Bacterial meningitis can be contagious depending on the cause.
Viral meningitis can be contagious depending on the cause.
Meningitis can be transmitted through coughing.
Meningitis can be transmitted through sneezing.
Meningitis can be transmitted through kissing.
Meningitis can be transmitted through sharing utensils.
Meningitis can be transmitted through sharing cutlery.
Meningitis can be transmitted through sharing toothbrushes.
Meningococcal bacteria can spread through close contact such as living with or caring for an infected person.
Infants are at higher risk for bacterial meningitis.
Teenagers and young adults are at higher risk for meningococcal meningitis.
Crowded living conditions (e.g., college dorms, military bases) increase transmission risk.
People with compromised immune systems are at higher risk.
People missing spleens are at higher risk.
Bacterial meningitis is treated with intravenous antibiotics.
Bacterial meningitis is sometimes treated with corticosteroids.
Viral meningitis is usually managed with rest.
Viral meningitis is usually managed with fluids.
Viral meningitis is usually managed with medication to manage pain and fever.
Antibiotics do not treat viruses.
Vaccination is the most effective way to protect against certain types of bacterial meningitis.
